sources.title: Federal Acquisition Regulation, Part 16, Types of Contracts
authoritativeFor: allocation of cost and performance risk
keyFacts: FAR Part 16 identifies a range of contract types intended to provide flexibility in acquiring supplies and services.
The contract types vary according to the degree and timing of responsibility and risk assumed by the contractor for performance costs.
FAR Part 16 states that a firm-fixed-price contract places maximum risk and full responsibility for costs and resulting profit or loss on the contractor.
Cost-reimbursement contract types generally place greater cost risk on the government and require appropriate surveillance and controls.
Contract-type selection is expected to reflect the specific acquisition and risk environment rather than a default preference alone.
sources.usageLimitations: United States federal acquisition regulation. It is not a universal commercial contract rule and does not provide legal advice. Reverify current text and consult qualified procurement and legal professionals for a specific acquisition.

sources.title: Federal Acquisition Regulation, Subpart 42.15, Contractor Performance Information
keyFacts: FAR Subpart 42.15 establishes policies and procedures for recording and maintaining contractor performance information.
Past performance information is relevant to future source-selection decisions in United States federal acquisition.
Performance evaluation records require controlled handling and appropriate process.
sources.usageLimitations: United States federal procurement context. Do not present the federal process as a mandatory commercial supplier-scorecard method. Reverify current requirements before professional use.

sources.title: Information and Communications Technology Supply Chain Risk Management Essentials
authoritativeFor: information and communications technology supply-chain risk
keyFacts: CISA treats ICT supply-chain risk management as a lifecycle concern rather than a one-time vendor-selection activity.
Supply-chain risk can involve products, services, suppliers, dependencies, counterfeits, malicious functionality, vulnerabilities, and disruption.
Organizations are encouraged to integrate supply-chain risk management into governance, acquisition, operations, and incident response.
sources.usageLimitations: Cybersecurity and ICT-specific guidance. Tailor to sector, risk, contracts, and organizational authority. Do not treat guidance as a legal determination.

sources.owner: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, Govern Supply Chain Risk Management Category
keyFacts: NIST CSF 2.0 added Govern as a core function and includes a Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management category.
The framework supports defining supplier and customer roles, requirements, risk processes, and monitoring in a cybersecurity context.
The framework is voluntary guidance and is intended to be tailored.
sources.usageLimitations: Voluntary cybersecurity framework. It does not create a universal legal requirement and should be tailored to applicable obligations and organizational context.
